planting.note: Root stem or leaf cuttings with at least one node in a fast-draining, perlite-enriched mix and keep barely moist until new growth signals rooting. Tricolor needs noticeably brighter light than plain green clusiifolia to hold its variegation, and new leaves that emerge solid green signal it is reverting toward the species type.

directions: Grow in bright indirect light with an hour or two of gentle morning sun in a well-draining, perlite-enriched potting mix, letting the top half of the soil dry before watering again. Tricolor is a variegated sport of Peperomia clusiifolia bearing thick, fleshy, spoon-shaped rosette leaves edged in irregular bands of cream and rose-pink over a deep green center, a more dramatic patterning than the plain red-edged species and one of the showiest color combinations in the genus. Like other clusiifolia forms its succulent leaves store water, making it tolerant of missed waterings but intolerant of soggy soil, and low light will cause the pink and cream tones to fade as growth reverts toward solid green. Its compact, upright rosette habit suits windowsills, desks, and mixed succulent-style houseplant displays, and it is non-toxic to pets.
sources: Missouri Botanical Garden Plant Finder — Peperomia clusiifolia
Costa Farms — Peperomia Tricolor Care Guide
ASPCA Animal Poison Control — Peperomia (non-toxic to pets)

planting.note: Divide rooted offsets or root individual leaf cuttings (petiole down) in a light, well-draining mix; Little Fantasy is slower and more compact than standard caperata cultivars, so expect a longer wait before divisions fill out. Keep the mix on the dry side, since its thinner miniature leaves are still prone to rot if kept wet.

directions: Grow in bright, indirect light in a light, well-draining potting mix, and let the surface dry before watering — Little Fantasy is a dwarf selection of the ruffled Peperomia caperata bearing small, deeply corrugated, heart-shaped, dark green leaves on short reddish petioles, staying only a few inches tall and wide at maturity, well under the size of standard caperata cultivars like 'Rosso' or 'Luna Red'. Its miniature scale and dense, tidy rosette habit make it a favorite for terrariums, dish gardens, and small pots on crowded windowsills where full-size peperomias would quickly outgrow the space. It shares the thin, easily rotted roots typical of caperata cultivars, so it is best watered thoroughly and then left to dry rather than kept continuously moist. Thin, wiry flower spikes may appear occasionally but are grown incidentally; the foliage is the ornamental feature.
sources: Missouri Botanical Garden Plant Finder — Peperomia caperata
North Carolina State University Extension — Peperomia caperata
American Gesneriad and Peperomia Society — Peperomia caperata cultivars

planting.note: Divide offsets from the clumping base or root basal stem cuttings in a light, well-draining mix; Flowering Peperomia is slower to establish than most trailing peperomias and prefers to be left undisturbed once settled rather than divided often.

directions: Grow in bright, filtered light in a humus-rich, well-draining mix, keeping the soil lightly and evenly moist rather than letting it dry out completely between waterings. Peperomia fraseri is a clumping Andean species grown as much for its flowers as its foliage — unlike most peperomias, whose thin flower spikes are inconspicuous, this species produces dense, upright, brush-like white flower spikes with a distinct sweet fragrance above rounded, deep-green, quilted leaves, earning it the trade name Flowering Peperomia. It prefers cooler nights and higher humidity than typical houseplant peperomias, reflecting its cloud-forest origin, and benefits from a humidity tray or terrarium-style enclosure in dry indoor air. Remove spent flower spikes at the base once bloom fades to keep the clump tidy and encourage further flowering flushes.
sources: Missouri Botanical Garden Plant Finder — Peperomia species
American Gesneriad and Peperomia Society — Peperomia fraseri cultivation notes
Steve's Leaves — Peperomia fraseri care guide

planting.note: Start dormant tubers in spring in a shallow pot of loose, well-drained, humus-rich mix, barely covering the tuber, and keep warm and lightly moist until the twining stem emerges; provide a moss pole or small trellis right away since the vine climbs quickly once growth begins.

directions: Grow in bright, indirect light in a well-drained, humus-rich potting mix with a moss pole or trellis for support; this South American tuberous vine (native to Brazil and Peru, sometimes traded under the synonym Dioscorea dodecaneura) is grown almost exclusively for its striking heart-shaped leaves, which are patterned in silver, green, and cream above with deep wine-purple undersides. Unlike the edible yam species in this genus, it is cultivated purely as an ornamental foliage houseplant or shaded patio specimen and is not grown for its small, saponin-rich tubers, which are not eaten. The vine is naturally deciduous: expect it to drop its leaves and go fully dormant for several months each year, at which point watering should be withheld and the tuber left dry and undisturbed in its pot until new growth resumes. Because it is frost-tender, grow outdoors year-round only in the warmest tropical zones; elsewhere overwinter the dormant tuber indoors in a cool, dark, dry spot.
sources: Kew Royal Botanic Gardens, Plants of the World Online (POWO)

planting.note: Grow in bright light with some direct morning sun in a very fast-draining, chunky succulent-and-epiphyte mix; unlike most hoyas this species grows upright and shrubby rather than trailing, so it needs little support.

directions: Native to Thailand and Laos, Hoya pachyclada stands apart from most cultivated hoyas by growing as a stiff, self-branching small shrub rather than a climbing vine, with thick, pale grey-green succulent leaves arranged in tidy opposite pairs. Clusters of waxy, star-shaped white flowers with deep burgundy-red centers open at the stem tips and rebloom from the same spurs for years, releasing a light sweet fragrance in the evening. Because the leaves store water like a succulent, this species is markedly more drought-tolerant than typical trailing hoyas and rots quickly if the chunky mix stays wet, so let it dry out fully between waterings. Bright light keeps the compact habit dense and encourages more frequent flowering than the lower light many other hoyas will tolerate.
sources: NSE Tropicals — Hoya pachyclada care guide

planting.note: Grow on a small trellis or moss pole in bright, filtered light in a fast-draining, chunky epiphytic mix; this Indonesian species is grown as much for its silver-splashed foliage as for its flowers.

directions: Hoya purpureofusca, native to Java, is grown chiefly for its dark green leaves irregularly splashed with silver flecking along twining stems that climb readily on a trellis or moss pole. Its umbels of small, reflexed flowers open in a dusky purple-brown shade with a fine fuzzy texture on the petals, a smokier and hairier bloom than the smooth pink or white flowers typical of many cultivated hoyas. The vine grows steadily in warm, humid conditions and flowers most reliably once stems have hardened and matured, so avoid hard pruning of older growth where flower spurs form. Let the chunky mix dry noticeably between waterings, since like most epiphytic hoyas it is far more tolerant of drought than of soggy roots.

common_name: Giant Red Star Hoya (Macgillivray's Wax Vine)

planting.note: Grow on a sturdy trellis in bright, filtered light with high heat and humidity in a fast-draining, chunky epiphytic mix; native to Queensland rainforest, it is a vigorous vine that needs a few years of growth before it flowers.

directions: Hoya macgillivrayi, native to the Cape York rainforests of Queensland, Australia, is prized among collectors for producing some of the largest flowers in the entire genus, with deep burgundy-red, star-shaped blooms that can span several inches across in dense, drooping umbels. Its large, glossy, dark green leaves grow on vigorous twining stems that climb quickly once established, but the vine typically needs two or more years of steady growth before it matures enough to flower. Consistent warmth, high humidity, and bright filtered light encourage the strongest bloom production, while cool or dry conditions can stall growth for extended periods. Keep the chunky mix evenly moist through the growing season and allow it to dry slightly at the surface between waterings to avoid root rot.

common_name: Wiberg's Miniature Hoya (Compact Dark-Flowered Wax Vine)

planting.note: Grow in a small hanging pot or on a mini trellis in bright, filtered light in a fast-draining, chunky epiphytic mix; a compact Philippine species well suited to crowded collector shelves.

directions: Hoya wibergiae is a compact Philippine species with small, thick, closely spaced leaves on short, densely branching stems, making it far more restrained in habit than sprawling species like Hoya carnosa. Its tight umbels of small, dark maroon-purple flowers form at the leaf axils and rebloom repeatedly from the same short spurs once the plant is established. The miniature size and slow, tidy growth make it well suited to small pots or crowded collector shelves rather than large trellised displays. Allow the chunky, fast-draining mix to dry between waterings, since its thick leaves store some moisture and resent constantly soggy roots.

planting.note: Grow on a small trellis in bright, filtered light in a fast-draining, chunky epiphytic mix; this Bornean species is grown for its silver-mottled foliage and small red-tipped flowers.

directions: Hoya erythrostemma, native to Borneo, carries dark green leaves patterned with irregular silver speckling similar to its close relatives in the sigillatis group, on twining stems that climb slowly compared to more vigorous species like Hoya australis. Its small umbels of pale cream to yellow-green flowers are topped with a strikingly red-tipped corona, the feature that gives the species its name. Growth is steady rather than fast, and the vine flowers most consistently once stems have hardened in a stable, warm, humid environment. Let the chunky epiphytic mix dry noticeably between waterings, as this species is more prone to root rot than to drought stress.

planting.note: Grow on a trellis or moss pole in bright, filtered light in a fast-draining, chunky epiphytic mix; native to Sumatra and Java, its leaves resemble cinnamon foliage in shape and venation.

directions: Hoya cinnamomifolia takes its name from its elliptical, prominently three-veined leaves that closely resemble true cinnamon foliage, borne on vigorously twining stems native to Sumatra and Java. Its umbels of star-shaped flowers open in a dusky purple-brown shade with sharply reflexed, fuzzy-textured petals, a smokier and hairier bloom than the smooth pale flowers of Hoya carnosa. The vine climbs readily on a trellis or moss pole in warm, humid conditions and reblooms from the same woody spurs once established, so avoid removing old flowering stems during pruning. Allow the fast-draining, chunky mix to dry between waterings to prevent root rot in this drought-tolerant epiphyte.

planting.note: Grow on a small trellis in bright, filtered light in a fast-draining, chunky epiphytic mix; a Philippine species collected chiefly for its silver-mottled leaves.

directions: Hoya siariae is a Philippine species grown mainly for its dark green leaves mottled with irregular silver blotches, a foliage pattern that draws collector interest much like Hoya sigillatis and Hoya lacunosa. Its twining stems carry small umbels of modestly sized, pale flowers that are secondary to the plant's ornamental leaves in most collections. Growth is slow to moderate, and the vine benefits from consistent warmth and humidity to maintain steady leaf production and the sharpest silver patterning. Let the chunky, fast-draining mix dry between waterings, since prolonged soggy conditions cause root and stem rot far more readily than mild drought stress.

planting.note: Grow on a trellis or moss pole in bright, filtered light in a fast-draining, chunky epiphytic mix; prized for large, intensely honey-scented flower clusters.

directions: Hoya meliflua, whose species name means honeyed, is a Philippine vine grown for its large, dense umbels of small cream to pale yellow flowers that release an intensely sweet, honey-like fragrance, among the strongest scents in the genus. The glossy, elliptical leaves grow on vigorously twining stems that climb steadily on a trellis or moss pole in warm, humid conditions. Established plants rebloom repeatedly from the same flower spurs, often producing dozens of blooms per umbel, so old flowering stems should be left in place rather than pruned back hard. Keep the chunky epiphytic mix well-drained and allow it to dry slightly between waterings to avoid root rot.

common_name: Curly Fireworks Rex Begonia (Spiral-Leaf Metallic Silver Sport)

planting.note: Grow year-round as a houseplant in bright, indirect light; if summering outdoors keep it in deep, sheltered shade and bring it back in well before nights drop toward 55F.

directions: Pot in a light, fast-draining mix and site in bright, filtered light with no direct sun, which scorches the thin leaf blades. Curly Fireworks is a curled-leaf sport of the classic 'Fireworks' rex begonia, producing narrow, twisted, metallic-silver leaves that spiral tightly at the petiole before flaring outward, giving a more sculptural, tousled look than the flat-leaved parent. Keep humidity elevated with a pebble tray or plant grouping, and let the topsoil dry slightly between waterings to prevent rhizome rot. Propagate by rhizome division or leaf-wedge cuttings taken at repotting time.

planting.note: Grow indoors year-round in bright, indirect light; move outdoors to deep shade only after nights stay reliably above 55F, and bring back in before fall temperatures drop.

directions: Grow in a light, humus-rich, well-drained potting mix in bright, filtered light away from direct sun. Jurassic Silver is a compact, vigorous rex begonia from the modern Jurassic breeding line, bearing broad, almost entirely silver-white leaves edged in a narrow band of dark green with red-tinted undersides, giving strong contrast in mixed foliage displays. Maintain elevated humidity and allow the topsoil to dry slightly between waterings to avoid rhizome and root rot. Divide rhizomes or take leaf-wedge cuttings in spring to propagate.

planting.note: Grow year-round as a houseplant in bright, indirect light; if moved outdoors for summer, keep in sheltered deep shade and return indoors before nights fall below 55F.

directions: Pot in a light, fast-draining, humus-rich mix and place in bright, filtered light out of direct sun. Jurassic Watermelon takes its name from broad, rounded leaves patterned in pink-toned silver with dark green rind-like margins, echoing the cut face of a watermelon; the pattern deepens in cooler, brighter conditions. Keep humidity elevated and let the topsoil dry slightly between waterings to prevent rhizome rot. Propagate by rhizome division or leaf-wedge cuttings when repotting in spring.

planting.note: Grow indoors year-round in bright, indirect light; if summered outside keep in deep, sheltered shade and bring back in before nights drop toward 55F.

directions: Grow in a light, well-drained, humus-rich mix in bright, filtered light away from direct sun. Jurassic Green is a vigorous, easy-care rex begonia bearing large, ruffled-edge leaves in rich emerald green overlaid with a metallic silver spiral zone near the petiole, offering a calmer, more monochrome look than the brighter Jurassic series members. Keep humidity elevated with a pebble tray or plant grouping and allow the topsoil to dry slightly between waterings to prevent rhizome rot. Propagate by rhizome division or leaf-wedge cuttings in spring.

common_name: Inca Flame Rex Begonia (Metallic Copper-Orange Spiral Rex Begonia)

planting.note: Grow year-round as a houseplant in bright, indirect light; if summering outdoors keep in sheltered deep shade and bring back inside before nights fall below 55F.

directions: Pot in a light, humus-rich, fast-draining mix and site in bright, filtered light out of direct sun. Inca Flame produces small, pointed, spiral-based leaves in glowing metallic copper-orange with a narrow dark-green rim, one of the warmer-toned entries among rex begonia cultivars and a strong accent against the more common silver-and-green forms. Maintain elevated humidity and let the topsoil dry slightly between waterings to avoid rhizome rot. Propagate by rhizome division or leaf-wedge cuttings taken at repotting time.

common_name: Cowardly Lion Rex Begonia (Cream-Edged Spotted Rex Begonia)

planting.note: Grow indoors year-round in bright, indirect light; if moved outside for summer keep in deep, sheltered shade and return indoors well before nights drop toward 55F.

directions: Grow in a light, well-drained, humus-rich mix in bright, filtered light away from direct sun. Cowardly Lion bears rounded, ruffled leaves edged in a broad band of cream to pale yellow surrounding an inner zone speckled with silver and green spots, a variegation pattern that gives strong two-tone contrast even in low light. Keep humidity elevated with a pebble tray or plant grouping and allow the topsoil to dry slightly between waterings to prevent rhizome rot. Propagate by rhizome division or leaf-wedge cuttings in spring.

common_name: Pewterware Rex Begonia (Metallic Pewter-Silver Rex Begonia)

planting.note: Grow year-round as a houseplant in bright, indirect light; if summering outdoors keep in sheltered deep shade and bring back in before nights fall below 55F.

directions: Pot in a light, fast-draining, humus-rich mix and place in bright, filtered light out of direct sun. Pewterware is named for its broad, flat leaves in a solid, dull metallic pewter-silver overlaid with fine dark-green veining, a subdued, textural look that reads almost like hammered metal from across a room. Keep humidity elevated and let the topsoil dry slightly between waterings to prevent rhizome rot. Propagate by rhizome division or leaf-wedge cuttings when repotting in spring.

planting.note: Plant this male-only vine within 30 to 50 feet of female hardy kiwi cultivars such as 'Ananasnaja' or 'Geneva'; it bears no fruit itself but is grown solely to supply pollen for a productive fruiting planting.

directions: 119-40B is a male hardy kiwi selection grown exclusively as a pollen source, since Actinidia arguta is dioecious and female vines set little or no fruit without a nearby male. It produces abundant, well-timed blossoms that overlap the bloom period of widely grown female cultivars, making it a standard pairing for plantings of 'Ananasnaja' and similar selections. The vine itself never fruits, so it can be pruned hard and trained on a modest support rather than a full production trellis. Site it centrally among several female vines for the most even pollination coverage.
